exercise.title: Add9: the 2nd on top of the chord
exercise.why: An add9 chord keeps its 3rd and adds the 2nd on top, so it still sounds major, where a sus2 chord gives the 3rd up.

cells.text:
Tap {{1}}, {{3}} and {{5}} on the staff below: the {{=key}} major chord, one note at a time. Tap them again and add the ringed {{2}} from the octave above: that is {{=key}}add9.
The added note is called the 9 because it is the 2nd counted on past the octave.
Practice until you can hum the added note before you tap it.

Press Play below to start the backing track: the plain chord, then {{=key}}add9, the plain chord again, then {{=key}}sus2, one bar each. In add9 the 3rd is still there; in sus2 it is gone.
Say "add9" or "sus2" as each one arrives, with the lit chord box to help.
Practice until you can tell which of the two still sounds major without looking.

The staff below builds the same chord from a new root, a 5th higher. Tap {{1}}, {{3}} and {{5}}, then add the ringed {{2}} from the octave above.
Practice until you can hum the added note before you tap it.
On the new root the notes are new, and the added note is still the {{2}}, an octave up.
